Here's a little trick to find fractions that approximate the square root of two.

We want to find m/n so that m^2 /n^2 is as close to 2 as possible. This implies m^2 = 2n^2 + 1 OR m^2 = 2n^2 - 1.

If n=1, 2n^2 = 2 which is one off from 1^2. Thus m=1, n= 1.

If n=2, 2n^2 = 8 which is one off from 3^2. Thus m=3, n=2.

n=3 and n=4 don't work.

If n=5, 2n^2 = 50 which is one off from 7^2. Thus m=7, n=5.

For any given combination (m,n), the next combination (M,N) can be found as a function of m and n:

M=m+2n; N=m+n.

So the series looks like (1,1); (3,2); (7,5); (17,12); (41,29); (99,70); ...

This converges pretty quickly to sqrt(2). 99/70 is as close as you'll get with both values under 100, and 99/70 - sqrt(2) = 0.000072.

The same can be done to approximate other values, though the algorithm will vary a little. For example, if we were going for sqrt(3), we start at (2,1) and (M,N) = (2m+3n,m+2n). This leads to 97/56, which is 0.000092 off from sqrt(3).

It comes down to one thing ... can the copyright holders prove financial harm has been done when a movie is downloaded without payment? And I'm not talking about proving financial harm in general across all downloads (which, by the way, is impossible to really prove), I'm talking about the individual being charged. Can the movie company prove that Mr. Jones would have paid for the movie had he not downloaded it from the Internet? In most cases, Mr. Jones will say that he would not have paid for a ticket to see the movie, and would not have paid for it on DVD, and would not have paid to download it. This being so (and why should the movie company's assertion be any more valid than that of Mr. Jones, who is in a position to know what he would and would not pay for?), no harm of any kind has been committed, and there is no reason or grounds upon which to seek redress.
